  <div class="wrap hero-in">
    <p class="eyebrow">Light transport research · RadianceLab</p>
    <h1>Caustics without<br>a <i>kernel</i></h1>
    <p class="thesis">A volumetric caustic through glass, solved in closed form. No neural network, no clamp, no denoiser — and blitzing fast. The sheet is exact; the pair that renders the frame above is consistent, not unbiased, and the number is on this page.</p>
    <p class="note" style="max-width:52ch;margin:14px 0 0;color:#9fb0ad">Above: a shaft of light meets a glass sphere and leaves its underside as a waisted horn. That image is the pair: computed on the sheet, gathered by the beam it hands off to. In the equal-pass A/B further down, this caustic's waist is 7.7 px wide where the kernel estimator's is 70 at r = 0.70 and, with the beam at the pair's own radius, 16.1 px.</p>
    <div class="spectrum"></div>
    <div class="stats">
      <div class="stat"><span class="k">Per pass</span>
        <div class="v"><span class="from">7.05</span><span class="arr">→</span><span class="to">1.17 ms</span></div>
        <div class="sub">after the vsync fix; 0.76 ms of it is estimation &middot; 217×140 film.</div></div>
      <div class="stat"><span class="k">Cone → MIS trio</span>
        <div class="v"><span class="from">6291</span><span class="arr">→</span><span class="to">1</span></div>
        <div class="sub">worst-pixel ratio vs reference.</div></div>
      <div class="stat"><span class="k">Hourglass solo → paired</span>
        <div class="v"><span class="from">0.976</span><span class="arr">→</span><span class="to">1.0000</span></div>
        <div class="sub">converged median against the beam at the same radius; by energy on the isolated caustic the pair reads 1.2 % above it.</div></div>
      <div class="stat"><span class="k">Equal-pass error</span>
        <div class="v"><span class="to">2.1×</span></div>
        <div class="sub">lower than the beam alone at 200 passes, on preset 51's fold.</div></div>
      <div class="stat"><span class="k">Analytic primitives</span>
        <div class="v"><span class="to">21</span></div>
        <div class="sub">kernel-free swept manifolds of 31 slots, plus six that carry a kernel (18, 19, 21, 28, 29, 30)</div></div>

<!-- ================= PROBLEM ================= -->
<section id="problem" style="--secc:var(--l400)" data-nav="Problem">
  <div class="wrap">
    <div class="narrow">
      <p class="sec-label">01 — The problem</p>
      <h2>A single grazing ray can ruin the whole frame</h2>
      <p class="lead">Volumetric caustics are the light that has already passed through glass before it scatters in fog. They are among the hardest paths in rendering: the light is focused to a thin, bright sheet, and almost no random path finds it.</p>
      <p>The usual answer is photon mapping — fire photons, store them, and gather with a kernel of radius <em>r</em>. That works, but the radius is a lie you agree to: it blurs the caustic and biases the answer, and shrinking it trades the blur for noise. This page is about refusing the lie and keeping the speed.</p>
      <p>An analytic estimator avoids the kernel entirely, but buys a new problem. Sweeping a photon into a surface and intersecting the camera ray with it introduces a <strong>Jacobian in the denominator</strong> — and when the camera ray grazes that surface tangentially, the Jacobian collapses toward zero and the estimator explodes.</p>
    </div>
    <figure>
      <div class="schem"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 640 360">

      <p class="note"><b>A photograph used to sit here, and it was pulled on 2026-09-08.</b> It showed the photon-cone estimator alone on preset 41 at 400 passes and its caption called the bright pixels the tangency locus, at <span class="mono">1189.8&times;</span> the scene mean. When every film on this site was regenerated from its own producer, that one did not come back: the estimator's own recorded config produces a frame with a twentieth of the shipped film's mean, and on this build the mixture that is supposed to fix it has the <em>higher</em> peak. The frames and the full retraction are kept in section 03 rather than deleted, but they are not evidence for this section's claim, so this section no longer shows them. <b>That the cone is the family's worst primitive is measured elsewhere and stands</b>: worst pixel against the reference, <b>6291 &rarr; 1</b> once it is mixed &mdash; the stat tile at the top of this page.</p>

<section id="idea" style="--secc:var(--l460)" data-nav="The idea">
  <div class="wrap">
    <div class="narrow">
      <p class="sec-label">02 — The idea</p>
      <h2>Sweep the photon into a surface you can intersect</h2>
      <p class="lead">A photon arriving at a scattering event still has unused degrees of freedom. Rather than committing them randomly and storing the result, let them sweep.</p>
      <p>Fix every dimension of a light path but two, and let those two vary. The scatter point traces out an analytic two-dimensional manifold in space — a sphere, a cone, a disk, a ruled plane. That manifold is a <strong>photon primitive</strong>, and a camera ray can be intersected with it exactly.</p>
      <p>The kernel disappears. In its place is a co-area Jacobian relating the swept parameters to the measure the camera ray actually integrates:</p>
    </div>
    <div class="formula">
      <div class="f">J = <span class="hl">|</span> ( ∂x/∂a × ∂x/∂b ) · d <span class="hl">|</span></div>
      <div class="n">One expression for every primitive in the family. The shape changes; the estimator does not.</div>
    </div>
    <div class="pair">

<text x="484" y="72" font-family="JetBrains Mono, ui-monospace, monospace" font-size="12" fill="#DDE3E0"><tspan fill="#FFD264">a</tspan> = ∂x/∂θ</text>
<text x="484" y="90" font-family="JetBrains Mono, ui-monospace, monospace" font-size="12" fill="#DDE3E0"><tspan fill="#FFD264">b</tspan> = ∂x/∂φ</text>
<text x="484" y="116" font-family="JetBrains Mono, ui-monospace, monospace" font-size="12" fill="#DDE3E0">J = |(a×b)·d|</text>
<text x="484" y="134" font-family="JetBrains Mono, ui-monospace, monospace" font-size="12" fill="#DDE3E0" fill-opacity="0.7">= t²sinθ·|ω·d|</text>
<text x="484" y="152" font-family="JetBrains Mono, ui-monospace, monospace" font-size="12" fill="#DDE3E0" fill-opacity="0.7">ω = (x−y)/t,  t fixed</text>
<text x="320" y="348" font-family="JetBrains Mono, ui-monospace, monospace" font-size="12" fill="#DDE3E0" text-anchor="middle">07 · photon sphere · sweep θ, φ</text>
</svg></div></div>
    </div>
    <div class="paircap"><b>Schematics</b><span>Left: the reference — a light point connected to a scatter point, no sweep. Right: the photon sphere — sweep the emission direction at a fixed free-flight distance and the scatter point traces a sphere about the light; the camera ray meets it at isolated points, and the two tangents at that point are the Jacobian.</span></div>
    <div class="narrow">
      <p>Because the manifold is exact, the estimate is unbiased with <em>no radius parameter at all</em> — the caustic is as sharp as the geometry, not as sharp as your kernel. What remains is the variance problem from section one, and it has an answer that costs nothing but bookkeeping.</p>
    </div>
  </div>
</section>

<section id="family" style="--secc:var(--l500)" data-nav="Family">
  <div class="wrap">
    <div class="narrow">
      <p class="sec-label">03 — The family</p>
      <h2>One measure, twenty-one swept manifolds</h2>
      <p class="lead">Which two dimensions you sweep determines the shape. Twenty-one of them are built, and every one was divided against an independent reference before the next was started &mdash; the straight-line members against the next-event oracle to a median of 1.000, the dielectric members against the stochastic beam. The ratios are in the ledger; the one that lands off, the solo hourglass at 0.976, closes to 1.0000 paired. The roster below is the useful part of the space.</p>
      <p>Twenty-one is the count that closes the picker: thirty-one slots, less the three baselines that are ordinary sampling, the six kernel estimators, and the one slot that is a rasterised gather rather than an estimator. Earlier versions of this page said nineteen, then twenty-two, and its siblings said twenty; none of those closed against the roster as it is filed today, and the discrepancy is what caused them all to be re-derived. <b>The kernel class used to be two</b> &mdash; the tracer beam and the tracer point. Section 04b is where three more arrived, and why they had to. The sixth is the hourglass pair, filed with them on 2026-09-08: analytic on its sheet, it carries the beam's radius everywhere else, and section 05 measures what that radius does to its energy.</p>
    </div>

    </figure>
    <div class="narrow">
      <p class="note"><b>The design criterion that mattered:</b> Jacobian flatness first, evaluation cost second, ease of connection third. A primitive that is cheap but singular everywhere is worth less than one that is expensive and well-conditioned — because in a mixture, the singular member is the one that poisons the estimate.</p>
    </div>

</section>

<!-- ================= MIS ================= -->
<section id="mis" style="--secc:var(--l540)" data-nav="MIS">
  <div class="wrap">
    <div class="narrow">
      <p class="sec-label">04 — Why a diverse set wins</p>
      <h2>The singular estimator down-weights itself</h2>
      <p class="lead">Each primitive has a grazing locus. The observation that makes the family usable is that <em>they are in different places</em>.</p>
      <p>Where one primitive's Jacobian collapses, another's is well-conditioned — and the balance heuristic weights each sample by how well every strategy could have generated it. The member that is about to produce a firefly is precisely the member that assigns itself a low weight. The singularity does not need to be clamped, guarded, or clipped away. It cancels.</p>
    </div>

      <div class="pane"><span class="tag a">A · single plane</span><img src="data:image/png;base64," width="398" height="275" loading="lazy" decoding="async" alt="A single swept-plane estimator showing its grazing band"></div>

        <div class="row"><span class="lbl">Mean radiance — A</span><span class="val">0.12640</span></div>
        <div class="row"><span class="lbl">Mean radiance — B</span><span class="val">0.12642</span></div>

      <p style="margin-top:20px">Both images are unbiased estimates of the same integral, at the same sample count, and their means agree to four decimals — they are computing the same answer. One of them is usable. That gap is the entire contribution of the mixture, and it costs nothing but bookkeeping: the weights are closed-form.</p>
    </div>

    <div class="pair" style="margin-top:52px">
      <div class="pane"><span class="tag a">A · cone alone</span><img src="data:image/png;base64," width="597" height="425" loading="lazy" decoding="async" alt="Photon-cone estimator alone, showing bright firefly outliers at the tangency locus"></div>
      <div class="pane"><span class="tag b">B · direction trio</span><img src="data:image/png;base64," width="597" height="425" loading="lazy" decoding="async" alt="The same scene under the three-primitive direction MIS, with the outliers gone"></div>
    </div>
    <div class="paircap"><b>Withdrawn 2026-09-08 — this pair no longer shows a contrast</b><span>Preset 41, 400 passes, strategy 9 against strategy 13. The panes are what the two estimators render on the current build, and they are indistinguishable.</span></div>
    <div class="narrow">
      <div class="readout">
        <div class="row"><span class="lbl">Frame mean — cone alone / trio</span><span class="val">0.03829 / 0.03840</span></div>
        <div class="row"><span class="lbl">Peak ÷ frame mean — cone alone</span><span class="val">858×</span></div>
        <div class="row"><span class="lbl">Peak ÷ frame mean — trio</span><span class="val">1138×</span></div>
        <div class="row hi"><span class="lbl">Reduction shown by this pair</span><span class="val">none</span></div>
      </div>
      <p style="margin-top:20px"><b>What this readout used to say, and why it does not say it any more.</b> It read 1189.81 against 13.38, an 88.9&times; reduction. When <span class="mono">renders.py</span> was written and every film on this site was regenerated from its own producer, ten of the eleven came back byte-identical or agreed in energy to 3e&#8209;4 &mdash; and this one did not. The shipped <span class="mono">fireflies</span> film carried a frame mean of 0.21171 with 63&nbsp;% of its energy in ten pixels; the film that the recorded config actually produces has a mean of 0.03829 and 1.2&nbsp;% in its top ten, and at ten times the passes it still does. On this build the two estimators are indistinguishable on this preset, and the trio's peak is <em>higher</em> than the cone's. The numbers above are the two films measured (<span class="mono">py docs/tools/filmstats.py stats</span>, peak divided by frame mean); no film has been swapped, and the pair is left standing rather than deleted so that the retraction is where the claim was.</p>
      <p><b>The claim itself is not withdrawn &mdash; its illustration is.</b> The direction trio's variance reduction is measured on the roster, not on this frame: worst pixel against the reference, <b>6291 &rarr; 1</b>, the number in the stat tile at the top of this page; and the plane pair two panes up, which regenerates byte-identical, shows the same mechanism at <b>20.8&times;</b> on a scene where the grazing band is genuine. What preset 41 needs to illustrate it again is a scene whose tangency tail is real at 400 passes &mdash; a scene choice, not a new number, and it has not been made.</p>
      <p>The three direction-swept primitives share a conditional-given-<em>p</em> measure, which lets the common selection and area factors cancel before any weight is computed. Without that cancellation the mixture would not be tractable at all.</p>
    </div>

    <div class="narrow" style="margin-top:52px">
      <h3>Which mixture, at which light size — and the two predictions the rig overturned</h3>
      <p>The two mixtures are built for different regimes. The planes sample a point on the light, so they should improve as the lamp grows; the direction trio conditions on one light point, so it should lose ground as that point wanders. The variance study wrote the crossover down before anything was rendered: the planes overtake the trio once the emitter subtends about 35° at the ball. A second prediction sat beside it for the caustic: the vertex-seeded hourglass (22) overtakes the light-seeded one (20) at 35–41°.</p>
      <p>Presets 58–62 are one rig built to settle both: a glass ball in fog under a downward quad whose edge steps 0.2, 0.5, 1.25, 3.2 and 8.0 at constant power — 2° to 77° at the ball — with every cell timed, eight independent pass-batches per cell, and the energy checked against the camera walk at every row. <b>Neither crossover arrived.</b> The trio beats the planes at every size: by 43× on equal time under the smallest lamp, narrowing to about 1.3× at 77°, where the cost slopes carry a 10–30 % timing uncertainty and the equal-time margin is inside it — the per-pass ratio of 2.2× at that row is not. The light-seeded hourglass beats the vertex one at every size, by 236× down to 1.9×. Both trends run the predicted way, so the crossovers exist — beyond the rig, near an emitter edge of 9–10 for the airlight pair and further still for the caustic, where the lamp would be nearly half the width of the fog box. The miss was on the side the study trusted most: the trio's variance floor is 1.10 per pass, not 3.8, and it rises 1.35× over a 1,600× increase in emitter area, not 2×. Both corrections are written into the study beside the predictions they replace.</p>
    </div>
    <figure>
      <img src="data:image/png;base64," width="1100" height="419" loading="lazy" decoding="async" alt="variance/lightsize/fig_crossover.png" style="border-radius:10px;border:1px solid var(--line)">
      <figcaption><b>Equal-time variance against emitter size</b><span>Left, the airlight: three planes (12), the direction trio (13) and the cross-family mixture (26). Right, the caustic: the light-seeded hourglass (20) against the vertex hourglass (22), with the beam-paired 21 above them both at full transport and isolated to the caustic. The dashed line is where each crossover was predicted. Presets 58–62, 217×140 film, 640 and 2,048 equal passes per row; relative variance per pass times milliseconds per pass, so lower is better.</span></figcaption>
    </figure>

      <p class="note">Equal-time cost of one unit of noise for the three airlight estimators; the last column is the vertex hourglass's cost divided by the light-seeded one's. The cost slopes carry 10–30 % error bars (±0.35 on the trio and ±0.2 on the mixture at the last row), so the bottom row's equal-time verdicts are marginal and the per-pass ones are not. The three airlight estimators agree on energy to 0.1 % at every row, and all three read 2–3 % above the camera walk — every bit of that excess sits inside the glass ball's disc, where a swept estimator integrates fog along the unrefracted camera ray and the walk stops at the glass. Outside the disc they agree with the walk to 0.03 %. That is the one camera-leg convention the whole light-sweep family shares, and the camera-leg cap that complement mode switches on closes it.</p>
      <p style="margin-top:20px">The third column answers the question the two mixtures invite: why not both? <b>Strategy 26</b> mixes the three planes with the direction trio under one measure. The obstacle looked like a change of variables — the trio's densities are conditional on a light point, the planes' live on the light's area — and turned out to be bookkeeping: multiplying the trio's densities by the light-point selection density puts all six on the same light-area measure, the area factor cancels exactly, and the six weights are closed-form with no root-find. It has the lowest per-pass variance of the three at every emitter size and, from the third row on, the cleanest tail; it costs 1.2–1.8× the trio per pass because it draws six members rather than three and pays a shadow ray for every crossing that lands, and under the widest lamp it edges ahead on equal time, inside the timing uncertainty. It captures both regimes per sample. Masking its members down to the planes alone or the trio alone reproduces 12 and 13 bit for bit; the check that the shared measure is right is the energy, which agrees with 12 and with 13 to 0.1 % across a 1,600× range of emitter area. Use it when the light size is unknown.</p>
      <p>One bug came out of the rig, and it is on the page because the rig is what found it: inside the trio, the sphere and disk members cast no shadow ray while the cone did, so on preset 48 the trio read 1.25× the walk under a glass ball's shadow. Fixed the same day; the trio now reads 1.016, and the mixture inherits the fix.</p>
      <p><b>And the rig's own oracle is the estimator to beat.</b> The reference at every row was the camera walk's single-scatter next-event estimate: a free-flight-sampled scatter point and one shadow ray. Its variance was recorded and never tabulated, and it is lower than any swept member's at every emitter size — 0.35 to 0.67 per pass against the trio's 1.10 to 1.49, and 1.4 to 3.6× better on equal time. That is the honest boundary of this family. Sweeping a dimension of an area light's single scatter does not beat connecting to it; what sweeping buys is the mixture mechanism above, and the connections next-event estimation cannot make at all. Hold on to that sentence — the next section reproduces it exactly, on a different construction, and the section after that is where sweeping stops being optional.</p>
    </div>
    <div class="slot">Screenshot — H8 · presets 58 → 62 in order · Split A/B with strategy 13 on the left and 12 on the right · MinBounce 0 · 640 passes each · one frame per preset, framing the fog under the ball as the lamp grows</div>
  </div>
</section>

    <div class="narrow">
      <p class="sec-label">04b — The lattice's other half</p>
      <h2>Sweep <i>one</i> coordinate instead of two</h2>
      <p class="lead">A photon leaves a vertex with a direction and a distance: three numbers, <b>(θ, φ, t)</b>, in a frame at that vertex. Fix one and sweep two and you get a surface — the cone, the disk, the sphere, kernel-free and shipped since the first week. Fix <em>two</em> and sweep one and you get a curve. There are exactly three of those, and until this week only one of them was built.</p>
      <p><b>The construction is the user's.</b> The ring and the arc, the shared measure that mixes them with the beam, and the observation that closes the lattice are all theirs; what was added here is the transcription into the renderer and the gates below.</p>
    </div>

      <figcaption><b>The lattice</b><span>Top row, the two-dimensional members: a sheet, and the camera ray crosses it at a point, so nothing is blurred. Bottom row, <b>the one-dimensional group</b>: a curve, which a camera ray in three dimensions misses, so each carries a one-dimensional kernel of half-width <b class="mono">r</b> and the white ring marks closest approach rather than a crossing. Read the figure by column: each pair is complementary — the sheet above holds exactly the coordinate the curve below sweeps.</span></figcaption>
    </figure>

    <div class="narrow">
      <h3>One expression, not three constructions</h3>
      <p>Every member of the bottom row is the same integrand times the same kernel <span class="mono">1/(2r)</span>, divided by one geometric term: <span class="mono">|(∂x/∂u) × d|</span>, where <span class="mono">u</span> is whichever coordinate is being swept and <span class="mono">d</span> is the camera direction. <b>The tracer beam's familiar 1/sin θ is that expression for a unit-speed sweep.</b> The beam was written first and looked like a special case; it is the <span class="mono">t</span> column of a lattice that now closes. The <b>ring</b> (strategy 28) sweeps φ, so its locus is a circle of radius <span class="mono">t sin θ</span> about the frame axis; the <b>arc</b> (29) sweeps θ, so its locus is a half-circle of radius <span class="mono">t</span> about the vertex itself. Write the volume element as <span class="mono">t² dt dμ dφ</span> and the point source's <span class="mono">1/t²</span> cancels it, which is why the ring carries one factor of <span class="mono">1/t</span> that the beam does not, and the arc carries that plus an explicit sine.</p>

      <h3>Ray versus circle is a quartic — and the primitive is a torus</h3>
      <p>Intersecting a camera ray with a circle of tube radius <span class="mono">r</span> is ray-versus-torus, which is what these primitives actually are, and the stationary-point condition squares to a quartic. Two things make the shipped solver simpler than the textbook one. The bracket is free and exact — every stationary point lies in <span class="mono">[−k−ρ, −k+ρ]</span> — and inside that bracket the quartic's own derivative is a cubic in closed form, whose real roots cut the interval into at most four monotone pieces, each sign change bisected. No companion matrix, no eigenvalues, <b>and no threshold to guess</b>.</p>
      <p>The part that is easy to get wrong is that you must <b>sum every stationary point</b>, minima and saddles alike. Two or three roots occur on <b>57.01 %</b> of hits when the camera ray runs near coplanar with the ring's circle — 51.15 % two-root and 5.86 % three-root over 165,429 measured hits — and those are precisely the configurations the primitive exists for. Keeping only the nearest root would have deleted the geometry the estimator was built to reach, and would have looked like a mild darkening rather than a bug.</p>

      <h3>The consequence that matters: the swept density stops cancelling</h3>
      <p>In the two-dimensional members the sampling density of the swept coordinate cancels against the emission profile, so the profile is divided out and never evaluated. Sweep one coordinate and it does not cancel, and that single fact sets the whole character of the group. The emission profile has to be <b>evaluated at the crossing</b> — which is why any of these is identically zero at a smooth dielectric (a two-dimensional delta integrated over one dimension is still a delta), and equally why an evaluated payload is exactly what would let a one-dimensional member carry a bounce off a <em>rough</em> surface. A delta in one angle is fine, and the family already ships it: the cone is the polar-delta ring.</p>
      <p class="note"><b>A corollary that was run as written on 2026-09-08, and half of it fell.</b> If the emission profile is axisymmetric about the frame axis, the ring's swept coordinate <em>is</em> the symmetry coordinate, and a μ-density shaped like the profile absorbs it entirely — <span class="mono">f_e / q</span> is a constant and the profile is never evaluated. That is why the frame axis is the light normal: a Lambertian emitter is axisymmetric about it by construction. Until 2026-09-08 this note cited a <span class="mono">cos⁴</span> lobe reading 1.0087 ± 0.0184 as the verification; that run sampled μ uniformly and <em>evaluated</em> the profile at the crossing — the opposite experiment. Run with the absorbing sampler (<span class="mono">run_lobe_absorb.py</span>, μ ~ 5μ⁴, same seed and N) the ring reads 0.987 ± 0.017, 1.018 ± 0.008 and 0.983 ± 0.011 on the broadside, steep and along-axis cameras — unbiased, like the evaluated one — with 1.2×, 2.6× and 2.5× <em>less</em> variance. On the near-tangent camera it has <b>20× more</b>: the absorbing density rarely visits the μ ≈ 0 rings the profile is dark on and pays them full weight, which is exactly where the ring's tangency family lives. The corollary is right about the profile and wrong about "pays nothing": where the singular family sits in the profile's dark, evaluating is the cheaper deal, and the shipped ring evaluates.</p>

      <h3>Three tangency families, and none of them overlap</h3>
      <p>The ring goes singular where the camera ray is coplanar with its circle. The arc goes singular where the ray runs along the frame axis. <b>The beam goes singular nowhere</b> — its parallelism needs two <em>fixed</em> directions to line up by coincidence, while a swept circle hunts the tangency. That disjointness is the argument for mixing them, and it is visible one derivation earlier than any film: at 800,000 samples per cell against a quadrature reference the ring alone reads <b>2.1323 ± 0.0516</b> on a near-coplanar camera and unity everywhere else — an excess of 1.13 against a bar of 0.05, <b>22 sigma, resolved</b>. <b>Only half of that pair is a measurement, and the half that is not is marked.</b> The arc's along-axis cell reads 1.0286 ± 0.0269, an excess of 0.0286 against a bar of 0.0269 — <b>1.1 sigma, not resolved</b> — and it was bolded here as a measured family on the strength of its centre alone. The arc's tangency family is <em>indicated</em> by this table and <em>demonstrated</em> by its worst-pixel column below, 41.7 times its own frame mean against the beam's 5.9, and by the swarm picture. Nothing downstream leans on the cell: the mixture's case rests on the ring's 545.7 and on the arc's tail, both far outside their noise.</p>
      <p>Strategy <b>30</b> puts all three on one measure — arclength along the camera ray — and applies the balance heuristic from the section above. Two properties fall out. With one shared kernel radius the <span class="mono">2r</span> cancels identically in the weights, so the shared-width instinct buys the densities for free. And the contribution goes as <span class="mono">1/sin ψ</span> while the weight goes as <span class="mono">sin ψ</span>, so the product is bounded and at most one member can be grazing-singular at a time. No member has to hand its tangent in: the three tangents are just the spherical frame rebuilt at the crossing.</p>
    </div>

    <div class="narrow">
      <h3>What the mixture buys, in one column</h3>
      <p>Preset 60, 217×140, kernel radius 0.15, converged at 3,200 passes. The oracle is the camera walk's own single-scatter next-event estimate — strategy 2 with <b>min bounce 0 and max bounce 1</b>, the panel's bounce-isolation fields set so that exactly one scatter is accumulated and nothing else can enter the comparison. Its support is the whole frame, 30,380 pixels of 30,380, so every ratio here is a whole-frame ratio.</p>
      <div class="tw"><table>
        <thead><tr><th>cell</th><th>ratio to the oracle</th><th>median relvar / pass</th><th>p90 relvar / pass</th><th>ms / pass</th><th>relvar × ms</th><th>worst pixel</th></tr></thead>
        <tbody>
          <tr><td>18 · beam</td><td>1.0208 ± 0.0009</td><td>108.0</td><td>210.7</td><td>1.073 ± 0.062</td><td><b>116 ± 7</b></td><td>5.9</td></tr>

          <tr><td>29 · arc</td><td>1.0360 ± 0.0039</td><td>318.3</td><td>812.8</td><td>3.531 ± 0.320</td><td>1124 ± 102</td><td>41.7</td></tr>

      </table></div>
      <p class="note">Eight disjoint pass-batches of 400, differenced out of the cumulative films; <span class="mono">ms/pass</span> is a least-squares slope over a 640 / 1,920 / 3,200 / 4,480 ladder with the film writes discarded, run <b>three times per cell, interleaved</b>, with the run-to-run spread of the three slopes as its bar (4.4–9.1 %). Worst pixel is max over frame mean on the converged film. The last column propagates the <em>cost</em> bar only — a median relvar carries no standard error here — so those bars are floors on the uncertainty rather than the whole of it. Note that <span class="mono">SE(ratio)</span> and the relvar columns are different statistics and move in opposite directions as the kernel thins: the frame mean is carried by a heavy tail that <em>shrinks</em> with <span class="mono">r</span>. Producers: <span class="mono">ra_gate.py var</span> for the ratio, <span class="mono">ra_cost.py measure</span> for the cost, <span class="mono">ra_equaltime.py</span> for their product and <span class="mono">ra_worst.py</span> for the last column &mdash; each stores its json beside the others in <span class="mono">docs/ring-arc/harness/ra_gate/</span>.</p>
      <p><b>The last column is the whole thesis in one number.</b> The mixture's worst pixel is 109× better than the ring's, 8.3× better than the arc's — and lower than the plain beam's own. The balance weight down-weights each member exactly where that member is about to go singular, and no member is singular where another one is. Per pass it is 2.7× better than the best single member at <span class="mono">r = 0.15</span> and 2.5× at <span class="mono">r = 0.05</span> (39.0 against 106.4; 118.2 against 300.2) — <b>at three draws per pass against that member's one</b>: the ring draws its own (μ, t), the arc its own (φ, t), and the beam sweeps the frame's direction, so a pass of the mixture is three light paths. Per draw, 39.0 × 3 = 117 sits beside the beam's 108.0 — parity — and each draw costs 2.3× the beam's, which is why the equal-time column below, not this one, is the verdict. It is also the only cell whose ratio matches the beam's converged value to four digits with the smallest standard error in the column.</p>
    </div>

    <div class="narrow">
      <h3>Consistent, not unbiased — and the number that says how much</h3>
      <p class="note" style="border-color:var(--l680)"><b>The caveat travels with the estimator.</b> At a finite radius the three members deposit on manifolds a radius apart, so the balance weights do not sum to one pointwise. <b>Strategy 30 is CONSISTENT, NOT UNBIASED.</b> It converges as <span class="mono">r → 0</span> and nowhere else, and it must never be called unbiased. That is also why complement mode refuses it as a primary <em>by name</em>: comp mode's claim is that the two layers together are the whole transport, and a primary that owns a box and then mis-reports its total breaks that claim at every radius the mode is actually run at. Its two members, 28 and 29, are each a single blur-biased estimator of the same box exactly as the beam is, and are not refused.</p>
      <p class="note" style="border-color:var(--l680)"><b>Since 2026-09-09 the caveat has a mechanism.</b> The kernel half-width is one control for the whole biased family &mdash; the <b>Blur width</b> group, shown for every strategy whose class-table kernel bit is set (18, 19, 21, 28, 29, 30) and for the surface map, hidden for the kernel-free rest &mdash; and it carries an opt-in progressive shrink, <span class="mono">pp.blurShrink</span> = &beta;, under which pass <i>i</i> reads <span class="mono">pp.beamRadius</span>&middot;<i>i</i><sup>&minus;&beta;</sup>. Within a pass every member of 30 still shares one <i>r</i>, so the 2<i>r</i> cancellation above is untouched; the running mean over passes is then the progressive estimator, and &ldquo;consistent as <i>r</i> &rarr; 0&rdquo; is something the renderer does rather than something the spec says. Measured on this preset at <i>r</i><sub>0</sub> = 0.30, &beta; = 1/3: the trio&rsquo;s excess over the beam plateau falls from +0.0036 &plusmn; 0.0003 at a fixed radius to inside the protocol&rsquo;s bar by 6,400 passes, and the ring&rsquo;s from 0.34 to 0.0125 &plusmn; 0.0046, with the derivation&rsquo;s &beta;* = 1/(2<i>p</i>+<i>d</i>) = 1/3 for the tube consistent with the observed slopes. Default &beta; = 0: every existing film is byte-identical. The numbers and their producer are in <span class="mono">docs/ring-arc/SPEC.md</span> &sect;3.1 and <span class="mono">docs/tools/blur_shrink.py</span>.</p>
      <p>The honest way to read a biased-by-design estimator is as a ladder, so here is the ladder — five kernel radii, 3,200 passes each, <b>every rung carrying its own error bar</b> from its own eight batches rather than one bar transplanted from a neighbour:</p>
      <div class="tw"><table>
        <thead><tr><th>kernel radius</th><th>18 beam</th><th>28 ring</th><th>29 arc</th><th>30 mixture</th></tr></thead>
        <tbody>
          <tr><td>0.300</td><td>1.0200 ± 0.0005</td><td style="color:var(--bad)">1.3506 ± 0.0183</td><td>1.0564 ± 0.0029</td><td><b>1.0233 ± 0.0004</b></td></tr>
          <tr><td>0.150</td><td>1.0208 ± 0.0009</td><td>1.1845 ± 0.0234</td><td>1.0360 ± 0.0039</td><td><b>1.0207 ± 0.0005</b></td></tr>
          <tr><td>0.075</td><td>1.0200 ± 0.0017</td><td>1.0902 ± 0.0155</td><td>1.0245 ± 0.0021</td><td><b>1.0197 ± 0.0008</b></td></tr>
          <tr><td>0.0375</td><td>1.0179 ± 0.0032</td><td>1.0556 ± 0.0101</td><td>1.0238 ± 0.0031</td><td><b>1.0199 ± 0.0015</b></td></tr>
          <tr><td>0.019</td><td>1.0209 ± 0.0033</td><td>1.0292 ± 0.0026</td><td>1.0214 ± 0.0040</td><td><b>1.0195 ± 0.0012</b></td></tr>
        </tbody>
      </table></div>
      <p><b>At r = 0.30, where the ring alone is 33 % high at eighteen sigma, the mixture is 0.33 % high — a hundredfold reduction, both terms measured, neither inferred.</b> And the 0.33 % is itself resolved at <b>7.5 sigma</b>, which is a change of verdict in the direction that costs us: with a per-rung bar the mixture <em>is</em> measurably biased at the widest kernel. That 7.5 replaces a shipped 5.1, and the correction runs the way that hurts. The 5.1 assumed the mixture and the beam were independent; batch <span class="mono">k</span> of every cell is the same block of pass indices, so they are not, and the measured batch correlation there is <span class="mono">ρ = +0.57</span> — the sign the construction predicts, since 30 <em>contains</em> the beam as an MIS member. A positive correlation means quadrature over-states the differential bar, so the shipped label was conservative and the honest one makes the bias more resolved, not less. That is the caveat above showing up as a number instead of a warning, and it is the right number to publish beside the payoff, because the payoff is unharmed. Below r = 0.15 the mixture is indistinguishable from the beam at every rung.</p>
      <p>The ring's excess, fitted rather than eyeballed over the four resolved rungs — 0.30, 0.15, 0.075, 0.0375, where the <em>whole-frame</em> excess clears twice its standard error — goes as <span class="mono">r<sup>1.067</sup></span> (+0.105 / −0.096, χ² 0.20 on 2 dof) — first order. <b>How far second order lies depends on the yardstick, and the yardstick is now named.</b> The headline is the profile-likelihood statistic — <span class="mono">√(30.67 − 0.20)</span> = <b>5.5 sigma</b>, delta-chi-squared — chosen because it evaluates the fit <em>at</em> p = 2 instead of extrapolating to it. The linear reading, (2 − 1.0670)/0.1055 = <b>8.8 sigma</b> — from the <em>unrounded</em> fit, which is the convention; dividing the rounded p and sigma gives 8.9, and that difference is arithmetic — is quoted for continuity and is no longer the one to cite: it runs a 68 % Monte-Carlo interval nine of its own widths into a tail it was never fitted on. Neither is a limit of the data — 0 of 20,000 refits reach p ≥ 2.</p>
      <p><b>Why first order rather than second is not settled, and the mechanism this page used to give for it has been withdrawn.</b> The obvious explanation is that a whole-frame average is dominated by the pixels where the ray is near coplanar with the ring's circle, where in general position the numpy model measures 2.4. That explanation needs the near-coplanar band to be the <em>low</em>-exponent region — low is what drags a frame average down to first order — and fitting the band and the rest of the frame separately puts the band's exponent <em>at or above</em> the rest's under both fitting conventions: 1.314 (+0.172 / −0.158) against 1.225 (+0.206 / −0.204) over the rungs resolved <em>within each subset</em> (three of them — 0.30, 0.15, 0.075 — the same rule as the whole-frame fit but on wider bars, so one rung fewer), and 1.571 (+0.121 / −0.105) against 1.322 (+0.155 / −0.144) forced over all five. The mechanism failed its own test, so it is withdrawn rather than softened. <b>What survives is the concentration, and it is measured</b>: the 5 % of pixels with the largest excess carry <b>64.5 / 63.5 / 60.8 / 58.2 %</b> of the frame's whole excess at the top four rungs, selected on four batches and scored on the other four so that the selection is not the noise being scored. The honest reason the split cannot decide it is that the mask is frozen at the <span class="mono">r</span> = 0.30 geometry while the real band narrows with <span class="mono">r</span>, so by 0.019 it holds 4.3 % of the excess instead of 60 %. A band that tracks <span class="mono">r</span> would be the experiment; it has not been run.</p>
      <p>Three labels moved when the bars were measured instead of carried, and all three are recorded: the &ldquo;unresolved&rdquo; mark on <span class="mono">r</span> = 0.0375 is <b>retracted</b> (1.5 sigma against a transplanted bar, 3.6 against its own); the arc's suspicious non-monotone rung turns out to be 0.20 sigma — it was the bar all along; and the ring's bottom rung, once &ldquo;exactly on the 2 sigma line&rdquo;, reads <b>1.7 sigma</b> once the batch correlation is measured rather than assumed away (<span class="mono">ρ</span> is <em>negative</em> for the ring, −0.44 at the top of the ladder, so quadrature was anti-conservative there). Unresolved rather than borderline. The paired ladder reads 17.8 / 6.9 / 4.5 / 3.5 / 1.7 for the ring and 13.8 / 3.7 / 1.6 / 1.4 / 0.1 for the arc, every other verdict unchanged, and <b>the exponent does not move at all</b> &mdash; <span class="mono">p</span> = 1.0670 on the independence-assuming bars and 1.0673 on the paired ones, 1.067 either way. (Until 2026-09-08 this sentence ended &ldquo;and the exponent moves by 0.001&rdquo;. That 0.001 was a grid artefact and not a measurement: <span class="mono">ra_fit.py</span> profiled <span class="mono">p</span> on a 0.0025-wide grid and reported its node 1.0675 as 1.068, while <span class="mono">ra_p2.py</span> used a grid ten times finer. Both scripts now share the fine grid, and <span class="mono">harness/ra_gate/p2.json</span> stores the whole derivation.) The caveat travels with it: eight batches give <span class="mono">ρ</span> a 68 % width of about ±0.45 and the paired standard error itself is good to about ±27 %, so neither 1.7 nor the 2.0 it replaces should be read to two digits — the point is that the rung is not resolved and that the shipped bar was the wrong estimator, not the wrong digit.</p>
      <p class="note">The whole column sits about 2 % above the oracle, and that offset is <em>shared</em>, not a property of the new members: the beam's row is flat in the radius at χ² 1.17 on 4 dof. It was tested on four fronts that could each have killed it. The sharp one is strategy 12, three-plane MIS, which has no kernel at all, finds its emitter by a different route, and renders byte-identically with the photon-lamp convention flag on and off — it cannot even read the flag the sweeps use, and it reads the same <b>1.0198 ± 0.0007</b>. Change the lamp and both move together, to 1.0336 and 1.0338 on preset 62. The statistic moves 1.4 percentage points across the light-size series, fourteen times its own bar, so it has discriminating power. The offset is a convention residue, it is preset-dependent, and it is not claimed to be zero.</p>
    </div>

    <div class="narrow">
      <h3>It loses to the plain beam on easy transport, and per draw it only matches it</h3>
      <p>Equal time, same rig: <b>290 ± 14 for the mixture against 116 ± 7 for the beam alone</b> — a loss of <b>2.51 ± 0.19×</b>. The mixture beats the two sweeps it contains — <b>1.52 ± 0.10×</b> the ring, <b>3.87 ± 0.40×</b> the arc, and a factor of ten on the arc's p90 tail — and it loses to the member that was already there. All three orderings survive their bars, which is why they are quoted with them. That is stated in the ledger and not buried. It is consistent with the family's thesis — <b>these primitives are heavier than plain sampling, and they win on hard paths, not easy ones</b> — but consistent is not confirmed: this group's hard case, a sharp emitter or an occluded lamp, has not been run, and until it is, the 2.51× loss is the whole of the measured verdict.</p>
      <p>Single scatter in clear fog with nothing in the way is the easiest transport this renderer has. The beam is the one member of the group that is singular nowhere, it costs 1.073 ± 0.062 ms per pass against the sweeps' 3.5–7.4, and on a rig with no obstruction it is very hard to beat — the same way the camera walk's next-event estimate beats every swept member of the airlight family one section up. What the mixture buys is not speed on that rig. It is that <b>it never has a worst pixel</b>, which is the property that matters the moment the geometry stops being easy: the ring's worst pixel is 545× its own frame mean and the arc's is 42×, while the mixture's is 5.0 — under the beam's own 5.9. A pixel like the ring's is not fixed by more passes. The ring and the arc sit inside the camera walk's own cost class — the walk costs 3.410 ± 0.567 ms per pass here, and they are 1.22× and 1.04× that — while the mixture is 2.2× the walk; the beam is 3.3× cheaper than the cheapest sweep, and the mixture is the only one you can point anywhere. <b>How well is that column known? To about 10 % within a session and about 1.6× between them.</b> It was re-measured on 2026-09-08 as three interleaved ladders on one binary, and the bars above are the spread of those three. The other number that has been quoted for it — a slope over the same eight batches' stored wall clocks, 0.73 / 6.90 / 3.38 / 15.13 — is not a competing measurement and not merely “load-contaminated” in the abstract: three of its four fits want a <em>negative</em> process start (−4.5 s, −5.1 s) where a real one is +0.3 to +0.9 s, two of its ladders are not monotone in the pass count, and at a matched 3,200 passes its renders ran anywhere from 0.61× to 2.05× the speed of tonight's — the machine moved inside the single sequential run that produced it. It does <em>not</em> swap the ring and the arc: that claim was wrong and is withdrawn, and all three measurements order the four members identically. Every ladder point now lives in <span class="mono">ra_gate/cost.json</span>.</p>
    </div>

    <div class="narrow">
      <h3>What it looks like</h3>
      <p>The <b>frozen batch</b> renders the whole one-dimensional group as geometry rather than as a film: twelve primitives per member, the sample pool frozen, 400 passes. Strategy 28 draws a swarm of <b>nested circles seen edge-on</b> — twelve rings coaxial about the lamp normal, stacking into horizontal arcs of increasing radius, brightest where the sweep is slowest. Strategy 29 draws twelve <b>open hooks</b>, half-circles about the vertex leaning at twelve different azimuths instead of stacking. Strategy 30 draws both of those <em>plus</em> straight streaks: rings, hooks and beams in one frame, and the trio is legible as a trio. No code was needed for any of it — the correlated-batch reconstruct path re-seeds after the camera prefix and calls the ordinary per-pixel sampler, which is strategy-agnostic by construction.</p>
      <p>The converged frames make the same argument a second and more useful way. At 3,200 passes the ring's film carries a <b>bright horizontal band of fireflies across the middle of the frame</b> — the locus where the camera ray is coplanar with its circle, exactly where the derivation says it must be. The arc's film carries a bright patch low and centre, on its own axis locus. <b>The mixture's film has neither.</b> The band and the patch are gone and what is left is the smooth fog gradient the beam and the oracle render. That is the disjoint-tangency argument as a photograph instead of a table.</p>
    </div>
    <figure>
      <div class="slot">Screenshot — H9 · preset 60 · correlated 2 · freezePool 1 · primCount 12 · 400 passes · step strategy 28 → 29 → 30 · same frozen pool each time · shoot the viewport only</div>
      <figcaption><b>Three frozen batches</b><span>The three members drawn from one identical sample pool, so the only thing that changes between frames is which curve the photon is swept into. This is the picture that makes the mixture's argument visible: rings, hooks and streaks in one frame, each dim exactly where another is bright.</span></figcaption>
    </figure>

    <div class="narrow">
      <h3>What the gates checked, and what was deliberately left out</h3>
      <p>The derivation gate was <b>re-run rather than inherited</b>, at 800,000 samples per cell against a composite Gauss-Legendre reference the estimators share no code with, and then again against an adversarial independent estimator that shares none of the algebra either — no quartic, no root find, no Jacobian, no <span class="mono">sin ψ</span>, just a tube indicator integrated by deterministic quadrature. The two rows that gate quotes &mdash; <span class="mono">A_broadside</span> against the isotropic lobe and against the tilted one &mdash; land within 1.2 sigma of unity on all three members. <b>Storing the adversary's whole twelve-row table on 2026-09-08 showed what quoting two rows had hidden</b>: ten of the twelve sit within about 5 % of unity for all three members and <b>two do not</b>. <span class="mono">B_steep/lobeT</span> reads 11.65 / 9.99 / 10.22 and <span class="mono">C_neartang/lobeA</span> reads 1.58 / 1.49 / 1.72. The disagreement is <em>common to all three members</em> &mdash; they agree with each other to about 15 % &mdash; which is not the shape of a member's Jacobian being wrong, and it is the only thing this estimator was built to test; both cells are anomalous against the quadrature reference too, and <span class="mono">B_steep/lobeT</span>'s reference is 4.549e-07, three to four orders below every other cell in the table. That reading is <em>inferred</em>: the settling experiment &mdash; shrink the tube, refine the quadrature, watch the two sides converge &mdash; has not been run, so those two cells are reported unresolved and <b>the adversary's verdict stands on the other ten</b>, not on all twelve. The <b>21 pinned films are byte-identical</b> across the change, and the pre-change set was itself verified 21/21 against the last recorded run before a line was written, so the baseline is a measurement and not an assumption. The bias-ladder film and the eight-batch film are 20/20 byte-identical, so the error bars cost no centre.</p>
      <p>Two panel behaviours are load-bearing here and worth naming. Every intersection the group makes runs through the estimator's shared options, so a <b>direction-preserving surface</b> is transparent to all three members: a passthrough wall lets the camera stand outside the fog box without any of them noticing, and unlike the three photon walks the group has no walk to relaunch, because it is a single segment from the light. And the group's shadow ray is applied to all three members rather than to the one that happens to need it, which is load-bearing rather than tidy: the supports must agree or the balance weights would be weighting a path class that one member cannot reach.</p>
      <p>When a strategy's scene requirement is not met, <b>the refusal is printed</b> under the Strategy combo in orange — what this scene lacks and what would fix it — rather than left in the log, because the symptom of an unmet requirement is a black frame and nobody hovers a control that appears to be working. The one-dimensional group declares that it needs both scene lights and a medium. Complement mode's <b>live ownership read-out</b> sits beside it and prints the resolved partition from the same declaration the runtime uses; it is the read-out whose needs bitmask was corrected on the <b>volume-light rig</b>, where two strategies had declared scene lights while their bodies actually looked for an emissive volume, so preset 43 would have been refused for the wrong reason.</p>
      <p class="note"><b>Not in version one, and said so plainly.</b> Single scatter only — all three are the first segment out of the light, which is why the mixture's beam leg is written locally rather than calling the shipped multi-bounce walk. No surface bounce yet, though the evaluated payload above is exactly the property that would allow one. No flexible subset dial: 30 is the fixed trio, and a mask for it would be four lines nobody has needed. And <span class="mono">Tr(t)</span> assumes the medium is homogeneous between the vertex and the crossing, which is exact for every fog box these run on. The obvious optimisation — a closed-form quartic solve in place of fifty bisection iterations — was <em>not</em> attempted, because the bisection is the version that is provably right and the cost is not out of range. <b>Which members that covers is a correction.</b> On the re-measured column &mdash; three interleaved replicates, <span class="mono">harness/ra_gate/cost.json</span> &mdash; the ring and the arc are 1.22&times; and 1.04&times; the camera walk's own 3.410 &plusmn; 0.567 ms per pass, inside its class; the <em>mixture</em> is 2.2&times; it. Until 2026-09-08 this page put all three inside the walk's class, on a cost column that had no stored artifact behind it.</p>
    </div>
  </div>
</section>

<section id="hourglass" style="--secc:var(--l580)" data-nav="Hourglass">
  <div class="wrap">
    <div class="narrow">
      <p class="sec-label">05 — The contribution</p>
      <h2>An analytic caustic through a glass sphere</h2>
      <p class="lead">Refraction is where analytic connections stop. A path that bends at two dielectric interfaces has no closed-form connection — which is why caustics have been left to photons and kernels. This one is not.</p>
      <p>For a spherical dielectric there is a symmetry that rescues it. Take the axis <code>a = normalize(C − y)</code> from the light through the sphere's centre. The entire refraction chain — entry, interior, exit — is <strong>rotationally symmetric about that axis</strong>. Rotating the whole chain is a rigid motion, so the exit rays sweep a surface of revolution: a waisted, hourglass-shaped caustic envelope that can be intersected in closed form.</p>
    </div>

      <figcaption><b>Schematic</b><span>The meridian chain at φ = 0 — emitted at polar angle ψ, refracted in at x₁, out at x₂ — and its revolution about the axis <code>a</code>. The exit rays sweep a waisted surface; the camera ray meets it where the white ring sits, and the two tangents there are <code>a × (x − y)</code> and <code>ω_out</code>.</span></figcaption>
    </figure>
    <div class="formula">
      <div class="f">J = <span class="hl">|</span> ( ( a × (x − y) ) × ω<sub>out</sub> ) · d <span class="hl">|</span></div>
      <div class="n">The co-area Jacobian of the swept exit surface. The fold dilation <code>det3</code> cancels per branch,<br>so the MIS weights are closed-form and O(1) — no root-finding anywhere in the estimator.</div>
    </div>

    <div class="narrow">
      <p>Two properties make it a result rather than a trick. First, the density <code>p = Σ p<sub>c</sub>·|J| / |det3|</code> was derived four independent ways and then <em>measured</em> against the sampler, agreeing to 1.0007. Second, as the index of refraction approaches 1 the hourglass degenerates exactly onto the photon cone — strategy 09 — which pins the measure convention against an estimator that was already validated. That limit matches to nine digits.</p>
    </div>

    <div class="pair">
      <div class="pane"><span class="tag a">A · kernel estimator, r = 0.70</span><img src="data:image/png;base64," width="398" height="275" loading="lazy" decoding="async" alt="The same caustic estimated with a large photon-gather kernel, visibly blurred"></div>
      <div class="pane"><span class="tag b">B · analytic pair, r = 0.15</span><img src="data:image/png;base64," width="398" height="275" loading="lazy" decoding="async" alt="Analytic volumetric caustic beneath a glass sphere in fog"></div>
    </div>
    <div class="paircap"><b>Preset 48</b><span>The acceptance scene: one glass ball, one point light, dark walls — built so the stochastic beam and the hourglass pair describe <em>exactly</em> the same transport and can be divided against each other. Both frames are 1000 passes over the same bounce range; the only difference is the estimator. B is strategy 21 at r = 0.15, its beam member included.</span></div>
    <div class="narrow">
      <h3>How much of the pair is still the kernel</h3>
      <p>The pair carries the beam's radius, so it has to be read the way strategy 30 is read one section up: as a ladder. Preset 48's caustic isolated to the pure transmit-transmit class (min bounce 2, max bounce 3), 217×140, eight disjoint batches of 400 passes per cell, and batch <span class="mono">k</span> of every cell is the same block of pass indices, so every ratio below carries its batch-paired bar. Producer: <span class="mono">docs/hourglass/hg21_ladder.py</span>, artifact <span class="mono">hg21_ladder.json</span>, run 2026-09-08. Energy is the currency: a kernel estimator on an open receiver blurs shape and conserves energy, so the energy column is the one to read.</p>
      <div class="tw"><table>
        <thead><tr><th>kernel radius</th><th>18 · beam alone, energy</th><th>21 · pair, energy</th><th>21 / 20</th><th>21 / 18 at the same r</th><th>21 / its own r = 0.0375 rung</th><th>18 / its own r = 0.0375 rung</th></tr></thead>

        </tbody>
      </table></div>
      <p class="note">Solo strategy 20 on the same isolation: 0.03463 ± 0.00002, the row every 21 / 20 ratio divides by. Energies are whole-frame mean luminance; ± is the standard error over the eight batches, and the two right-hand columns divide batch by batch. Re-run 2026-09-08 after the hourglass crossing solver went to double precision: the 18 cells are byte-identical, solo 20 rose 0.16 %, and every rung moved by 0.0005 or less.</p>
      <p><b>The beam alone is flat in its radius</b>, as a kernel estimator should be: 0.9982 ± 0.0022 and 0.9966 ± 0.0022 at r = 0.30 and 0.15 against its own r = 0.0375 rung. <b>The pair is not.</b> Its energy rises with the radius it carries, first order in r — +0.9 % at the radius every frame on this site is rendered at, +1.9 % at twice that, both resolved on the paired bar beyond argument. That is the structure complement mode refuses strategy 30 for as a primary: at a finite radius the beam deposits within r of the sheet while the hourglass numerator is evaluated as though the deposit were on it, so the balance weights do not sum to one pointwise, and the total the pair reports for its box moves with r. It vanishes only as r → 0, which is the definition of consistent. Its shape does not move: the energy in its brightest 1 % of pixels is 0.133–0.136 at every rung against the solo hourglass's 0.136, and on the Gate frame its waist is 7.7 px at r = 0.15 and 7.5 at r = 0.05. The kernel shows in the energy, not the width.</p>
      <p>What the pair buys is unchanged by this. The solo hourglass reads 0.25 % below the beam on this isolation (0.03463 against 0.03471), and a straight line through the four 21 / 20 rungs meets r = 0 at 1.004 — the guard's discards handed to the beam at weight one. Solo, the hourglass is kernel-free and discards. Paired, it discards nothing and carries a kernel. No shipped estimator of this caustic earns the word <em>unbiased</em>, and this site stopped using it on 2026-09-08.</p>
    </div>

    <h3 style="max-width:720px">Dispersion comes free</h3>
    <div class="narrow">
      <p>Because the estimator is parameterised by the refractive index rather than by a stored photon, making it spectral costs one substitution: draw a hero wavelength, evaluate Cauchy's relation, and let the beam and the hourglass share the same channel so the two techniques stay correlated. The caustic separates into a spectrum on its own — a dispersive volumetric caustic, analytic on the sheet and consistent as a pair, for the price of one line.</p>
    </div>
    <figure>
      <img src="data:image/png;base64," width="398" height="275" loading="lazy" decoding="async" alt="A dispersive caustic separating into a spectrum">
      <figcaption><b>Spectral</b><span>Dispersive glass under the paired estimator. The fan is the wavelength-dependent caustic; nothing in the estimator changed except the index.</span></figcaption>
    </figure>
    <figure>
      <img src="data:image/png;base64," width="398" height="275" loading="lazy" decoding="async" alt="Three glass spheres and two aimed mirrors casting caustics through fog">
      <figcaption><b>Relays</b><span>Three glass spheres and two aimed mirrors in fog. The light is reflected to a virtual origin before refraction, so a straight virtual chain stands in for the bent real one — mirror relays without a second bounce integrator.</span></figcaption>
    </figure>

    <h3 style="max-width:720px">How far the sheet can be pushed, and where it refuses</h3>
    <div class="narrow">
      <p class="lead">Three extensions landed after the hourglass itself, and they share a method worth naming before the numbers: each one asks whether some new transport is still a <em>rigid motion</em> of the same swept surface. Where it is, the existing quadric solver is untouched and the extension is exact. Where it is not, the estimator does not approximate &mdash; it refuses, by name, in the log.</p>
      <ul class="clean">
        <li><b>The refraction chain.</b> Push the sheet through a chain of glass balls instead of one. The revolution about the axis from the light to the first centre is a rigid motion of the <em>whole chain</em> if and only if every centre lies on that line — so a collinear chain costs nothing in the solver and a ball off the axis is refused rather than approximated. Which also makes it a <em>point</em>-source result: with a finite emitter the axis moves every sample, and the measured mean perpendicular offset for a half-0.4 quad is 0.395, with fifteen samples in a hundred thousand inside tolerance. The spec did not carry that correction; the measurement did.</li>
        <li><b>The post-ball mirror.</b> Light, ball, fog, then a mirror, then the eye. A reflection is an isometry, so the camera ray is reflected in the plane and the <em>same</em> quadric is solved against it; a root survives only when the bent path is real at every leg. It composes with the light-side relay and with the chain, and it is the one flag that turns the rasterised gather off — the screen bound projects the sheet where it is, not where its mirror image is seen.</li>
        <li><b>The glossy ring.</b> Strategy 24's reflection cone taken off the delta: the family's first vertex on a <em>rough</em> surface. A glossy vertex imposes no reflection law, so where every other member solves for the light point and the polar angle, this one samples both — five free dimensions rather than three — and evaluates the BRDF at every crossing rather than once.</li>
      </ul>
    </div>
    <div class="readout">
      <div class="row hi"><span class="lbl">Chain &mdash; variance per pass against the stochastic beam</span><span class="val">60.4&times; / 116&times; &middot; <span class="d">35.5&times; / 48.5&times; on equal time</span></span></div>
      <div class="row"><span class="lbl">Chain &mdash; energy on the caustic mask</span><span class="val">1.0023 &plusmn; 0.0061 &middot; 0.9966 &plusmn; 0.0068</span></div>
      <div class="row"><span class="lbl">Chain &mdash; the off-axis pair, same config</span><span class="val">film sum exactly 0.000000, one refusal line</span></div>
      <div class="row hi"><span class="lbl">Mirror &mdash; against the same scene from the eye's mirror image</span><span class="val">0.9979 &plusmn; 0.0017 by energy</span></div>
      <div class="row"><span class="lbl">Mirror &mdash; cost of the flag</span><span class="val">1.038 ms/pass (2.507 with, 1.469 without)</span></div>
      <div class="row hi"><span class="lbl">Glossy ring &mdash; against the camera walk on the same path class</span><span class="val">1.0005 &plusmn; 0.0088 at roughness 0.16</span></div>
      <div class="row"><span class="lbl">Glossy ring &mdash; variance per pass, three roughnesses</span><span class="val">2.22&times; / 3.13&times; / 2.61&times; &middot; <span class="d">6.6&times; / 8.3&times; / 6.8&times; on equal time</span></span></div>
      <div class="row"><span class="lbl">All three</span><span class="val">21 of 21 pinned films byte-identical with the flags off</span></div>
    </div>
    <div class="narrow">
      <p>Two of those rows say more than their numbers. The chain's refusal is the <em>acceptance criterion</em> for the whole approach: a scene the estimator cannot represent exactly renders as a black film and a named log line, not as a plausible picture that is quietly wrong. And the glossy ring's variance row falsified a written prediction &mdash; the design note said the ordinary camera walk would overtake the swept estimator as roughness rose, and it does not, at any roughness in range.</p>
      <p class="note"><b>What the ring cost, and why it is on this page rather than in a footnote.</b> Sampling the polar angle from a lobe-shaped density pins one coefficient of the shared cone quadric to exactly 1, at which point the leading term cancels in single precision and the estimator invents energy: measured at <b>81.5&times;</b>, <b>108.8&times;</b> and <b>8.7&times;</b> the correct value at roughness 0.05, 0.09 and 0.16. It is the sharpest illustration on this site of why every member is divided against an independent reference before the next is started &mdash; the picture at roughness 0.16 looked entirely reasonable while carrying nearly nine times the energy it should have. <b>And the defect was never the ring's alone.</b> Strategies 9, 13, 23, 24 and 26 solve the same quadric, and on 2026-09-07 the shared solver was reformulated &mdash; ray-centred, both differences of squares factored, the roots paired &mdash; and moved to double for every one of them; 27 keeps the separate double crossing it already had. Five of the twenty-one pinned films moved at 217&times;140 and 150 passes, and they are exactly the five that reach a cone. The direction was then settled by an arbiter that shares no line with either build, rather than by the fix arguing for itself: the quadric re-derived in exact rationals and cross-checked against mpmath at 120 digits, the two agreeing to <b>4&times;10<sup>&minus;39</sup></b>, run on the individual samples that moved. Six of the seven films move decisively onto it; the seventh moves by an ulp the other way with its maximum unchanged. The largest single change, <b>&minus;3.80&nbsp;%</b> on one preset-48 film, is <em>carried</em> by one sample at pixel (83,&nbsp;52) whose exact crossing lands 0.00275 outside the emitter &mdash; no light path, true contribution zero, and the 55.42 the old arithmetic paid it was invented energy. It is not the <em>whole</em> of the &minus;3.80&nbsp;%, and saying so was sloppy: the film sum moves 1135.22 to 1092.10, a net of &minus;43.12, so that single sample is <b>128&nbsp;%</b> of the net and the rest is paid back by pixels that <em>rise</em> &mdash; +9.72 at (102,&nbsp;61) and +2.38 at (90,&nbsp;56), the two places the Jacobian was too big rather than the root wrong. One number, two mechanisms, and they point opposite ways. One residual is open and is recorded rather than smoothed over: the solver builds its leading coefficient assuming the camera direction is exactly unit length, and on one near-tangency sample the shipped Jacobian is still <b>1.93&times;</b> the arbiter's, against the old form's 6.27&times;.</p>
      <p>One boundary is also now measured rather than assumed. A general, non-collinear chain was costed with a standalone harness that links nothing from the renderer and implements the crossing exactly as the specification describes it: <b>2 475&ndash;3 251 ns per footprint pixel</b>, 1.79 roots per pixel, a sheet covering 6.7&ndash;9.4 % of the frame. At the batch sizes this estimator runs, that is 188 ms per pass at the theoretical floor and 443&ndash;557 as implemented, against one-ball strategy 20's 13.1 &mdash; fourteen to forty-two times. The general chain is a <b>no-go</b>, and it is a no-go because somebody wrote the harness rather than because somebody estimated.</p>
    </div>
    <div class="slot">Screenshot — CHAIN: two collinear balls (preset 68) &middot; integrator mode 9 &middot; strategy 20 with Chain length = 2 &middot; Min bounce 2 &middot; 2000+ passes &middot; clean view (G) &middot; frame both balls and the waist between them; then load CHAIN: the same pair OFF-AXIS (preset 69) at the identical settings and shoot the black film beside the console line reading [PP][hgchain] REFUSED</div>
    <div class="narrow">
      <p class="note"><b>The second half of that shot is the point.</b> An estimator that renders nothing, loudly, on a scene it cannot represent is worth more than one that renders something on every scene. It is the same standard as the projection self-check on <a href="the-camera-is-not-a-viewpoint.html" style="color:var(--l680)">The camera is not a viewpoint</a>, arrived at independently in a different part of the estimator: refuse rather than approximate, and say which line refused.</p>
    </div>
  </div>
</section>

<!-- ================= HOURGLASS FLAVOURS (new section, slots after #hourglass) ================= -->
<section id="flavours" style="--secc:var(--l600, #EDA457)" data-nav="Flavours">
  <div class="wrap">
    <div class="narrow">
      <p class="sec-label">05b — The hourglass as a system</p>
      <h2>One member exists. The family is finite.</h2>
      <p class="lead">The refraction chain through a glass sphere has exactly three free parameters, and a camera ray consumes exactly two of them. That single fact enumerates every analytic hourglass there can be.</p>
      <p>Write the chain as <code>y → x₁ → x₂ → x</code>: a light point, an entry point on the sphere, an exit point, a scatter point in fog. Given the emitted direction — polar angle <code>ψ</code> about the axis <code>a = normalize(C − y)</code> and azimuth <code>φ</code> — both refractions are deterministic, and the exit ray is one line. Add the exit distance <code>r</code> and the whole chain is a map <code>(ψ, φ, r) → x</code>. A camera ray is a 1-manifold in R³, so meeting it costs two parameters. Therefore:</p>
    </div>
    <div class="formula">
      <div class="f">sample <span class="hl">one</span> of { ψ, φ, r } · sweep the other <span class="hl">two</span> · intersect the camera ray</div>
      <div class="n">Every analytic member has this shape. The stochastic members (18, 19) sample more and pay with a kernel.</div>
    </div>

      <figcaption><b>Flavours</b><span>Rows are members, columns are the three chain parameters. A red dot is <em>sampled</em>, a yellow arc is <em>swept</em>, a grey square is a kernel. Only two rows are in the engine; the fixed-apex form that the derivation started from exists in Python only.</span></figcaption>
    </figure>
    <div class="narrow">
      <p>The member that ships samples <code>cos ψ</code> uniformly on the cap and sweeps the revolution <code>φ</code> and the exit distance <code>r</code> — <em>"φ is never sampled; the revolution is consumed by the incidence."</em> Its density is <code>p = p_c · |J| / |det3|</code> per branch, and its <code>ior → 1</code> limit collapses onto the photon cone, which is how the measure was pinned.</p>
      <p>What makes the family worth building rather than admiring is the same thing that made the three-plane and direction-trio mixtures work: <strong>every row has a different singular locus on the same transport.</strong> The revolution form folds at the caustic waist; the meridian form folds along its own half-plane; the exit-distance shell is singular where the camera ray grazes a closed surface; the fixed-apex cone is singular at its own tangency. Under a balance heuristic the member about to misbehave is the member that down-weights itself. And each missing member arrives with its acceptance test already written — its <code>ior → 1</code> collapse lands on a primitive that is already validated (the meridian sheet onto the disk, the shell onto the photon sphere).</p>
      <p class="note"><b>On the word "tridirectional".</b> For the shipped member alone it overclaims: the dielectric vertex is <em>derived</em> from the light-side sample by Snell's law, not seeded, so the honest count is two subpaths joined at a derived vertex. It becomes literally accurate for the surface-seeded member — sample a coordinate of the entry point on the sphere and hang the light connection and the swept exit off it: <em>three independently parameterised pieces — light, the two-segment dielectric chain, sensor — joined at two constraints.</em> Used for the family, and defined on first use, it is a definition rather than a misuse.</p>
    </div>
  </div>
</section>

<!-- ================= TWO HOURGLASSES (slots after #flavours, before #surfaces) ================= -->
<section id="vertex" style="--secc:var(--l580)" data-nav="Vertex hourglass">
  <div class="wrap">
    <div class="narrow">
      <p class="sec-label">05c — The other hourglass</p>
      <h2>Seed at the glass, not at the light</h2>
      <p class="lead">The shipped hourglass keeps its free angle on the light side and derives the entry point. Turn that around — sample the entry point on the glass and an incoming angle about its normal — and you get a simpler object with a different reach.</p>
      <p>Sample <code>x₁</code> on the ball and a polar angle <code>θ_in</code> about the normal <code>n(x₁)</code>. Snell fixes <code>θ_out</code>; incident and refracted rays share one azimuth. Revolving that azimuth sweeps two cones apex-to-apex at <code>x₁</code>. For a sphere the normal passes through the centre, so the revolution is a symmetry of the ball and the whole chain — entry, chord, exit — rotates rigidly. The exit rays sweep a surface of revolution about <code>C–x₁</code>, and the camera ray meets it by the same revolved-quadric solve the first hourglass already uses.</p>
    </div>

      <figcaption><b>Schematic</b><span>The seeded vertex <code>x₁</code> (red), its incident cone opening into air, the chord and exit family revolved about the axis through <code>C</code>, and the camera ray meeting the exit sheet in fog. At the crossing azimuth the incident ray is <em>one</em> ray — so it is traced back, and here it hits the emissive quad.</span></figcaption>
    </figure>
    <div class="narrow">
      <p>That last clause is the whole story of when this member applies. Count dimensions: <code>x₁</code> (2) + <code>θ_in</code> (1) = 3 sampled, and the camera ray consumes the two swept ones. Nothing is left for the light side. With an <strong>area emitter</strong> the incident ray simply hits it; with <strong>fog before the glass</strong> it becomes a beam to connect along — a double-scatter caustic nothing renders analytically today. With a <strong>point light</strong> a single ray cannot hit, and the classic single-scatter caustic has no analytic vertex-seeded member at all. That class belongs to the light-seeded hourglass — which is exactly what its axis-revolution trick buys. The two are complementary, and the availability matrix by surface type and medium per side is written out in <code>docs/hourglass/VERTEX-HOURGLASS.md</code>.</p>
      <div class="readout">
        <div class="row"><span class="lbl">Same chain code as strategy 20</span><span class="val">seed and axis differ, nothing else</span></div>
        <div class="row"><span class="lbl">Strategy 20 refactored through the shared helper</span><span class="val">byte-identical — three pinned films (a1d4977f · fa75b2f1 · 6b070490) reproduced</span></div>
        <div class="row hi"><span class="lbl">22a / 20 on the shared class, presets 47 · 52</span><span class="val">energy 22a/20 = 1.0066 · 1.0195; 22a/18 = 0.9886 · 1.0046 (20/18 = 0.982 · 0.986 on the same support)</span></div>
      </div>

      <h3>Two cones at the vertex — the form that was actually meant</h3>
      <p>The member above is not quite the sketch it came from. Seeded at the <em>entry</em>, it lets the camera meet the exit family only after a <em>second</em> refraction — so the sheet is a hyperboloid whose waist sits out in the fog, not at any vertex. The sketch had the waist <strong>at the sampled vertex</strong>, and that is a cleaner object: given <code>θ_in</code>, the interface law fixes <code>θ_out</code> and the two directions share an azimuth, so the admissible pairs are exactly two cones apex-to-apex at the vertex — same side and same angle for reflection, opposite sides and different angles for refraction. The camera meets the <em>outgoing cone itself</em>, and a cone's intersection and Jacobian are strategy 9's, verbatim, with the apex moved onto the glass.</p>
    </div>

      <p><b>What the two cone members measured.</b> Both converge to 20's energy — 23/20 reads 1.000 once its tail has settled (48k passes against 20's converged 12k) and inherits 20's ~1% residual against the beam to four digits — but standalone, the exit cone is <em>not</em> the more efficient member: at equal passes it lights 50–60% as many pixels as 20 with the heaviest tail of the three (its worst pixel 20× 20's), and its own 12k/48k ratio is 0.985. The reflection cone is the real gain: it is the first analytic member of the <code>L S<sub>refl</sub> V E</code> class, matches the beam's reflection branch at 0.998 on a single glass ball, and fills 1.5× the beam's pixels. The variance study says why — the vertex members are light-trace-limited, and the exit cone also pays a chord back through the glass. Its remaining case is the {20, 22a, 23} mixture: three members with <em>different</em> singular loci (waist fold, sheet tangency, cone tangency), untested until the shared-measure ledger lands.</p>
      <p class="note" style="margin-top:22px"><b>This is the member that earns the word "tridirectional".</b> Light subpath, sensor subpath, and the two-segment dielectric chain seeded independently and joined at two constraints. Used for the family, defined on first use, it is a definition rather than a claim about connection edges.</p>
    </div>

</section>

      <p class="sec-label">05c — Surfaces</p>
      <h2>The reference denominator comes first</h2>
      <p class="lead">Every primitive above was certified by one number: its median ratio against an independent estimator of the same integral, converging to 1.000. Surfaces had no such estimator to divide by. So the first surface code in the integrator is not an estimator — it is the thing estimators will be divided against.</p>
      <p>At an opaque, non-emissive hit in the camera walk, make <strong>one</strong> Lambertian light connection using exactly the light set and sampling densities the medium estimators use, and stop. No continuation bounce. Mirrors and glass are untouched; the walk still terminates where it did. It is a reference, deliberately, and it is switched off by default so that every previously validated number remains bit-for-bit reproducible.</p>
    </div>

      <p style="margin-top:20px">The comparison needed a small piece of plumbing that did not exist: a headless control for the environment light. The test scene is an open-fronted Cornell box, and sky light reaching its walls is a path class the integrator has no emitter for — so it had to be zero on both sides, or the ratio would have measured the sky rather than the estimator.</p>
      <h3>What the footprint idea actually requires</h3>
      <p>The obvious surface primitive — intersect the swept photon sheet with a wall, get a footprint, evaluate where the camera ray lands — cannot be an estimator. Count dimensions: three unknowns, four equations. A 2-manifold sheet meets a 2-manifold receiver in a <em>curve</em>, and the camera's hit point is almost surely not on it. That missing dimension is exactly what a photon-map radius has always been buying.</p>
    </div>
    <figure>
      <div class="schem"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 640 360">
