      <figcaption><b>Footprint</b><span>Left: sheet ∩ receiver is a curve; the camera hit is off it, so no gather exists. Right: give the camera a sheet too, and curve ∩ curve is a point. The co-area factor is the triple product of the two sheet normals and the receiver normal — the surface analogue of <code>|N·d|</code>.</span></figcaption>
    </figure>
    <div class="narrow">
      <p>The repair is symmetric: give the camera a sheet as well. Two curves in a 2-manifold meet in isolated points, and the Jacobian is <code>det[N_p, N_c, n_S]</code>. Both incidence cosines land in the <em>numerator</em>, so grazing drives the weight to zero rather than infinity — the opposite of the medium primitives' failure mode. It also has a closed-form density in both directions, which is the admission ticket to the MIS network. That is the next estimator; the reference above is what it will be divided by.</p>
    </div>
  </div>
</section>

<!-- ================= VARIANCE (slots after #surfaces, before #proof) ================= -->
<section id="variance" style="--secc:var(--l460)" data-nav="Variance">
  <div class="wrap">
    <div class="narrow">
      <p class="sec-label">05d — When does an estimator work well</p>
      <h2>The variance has exactly three sources</h2>
      <p class="lead">"Planes work when they face you" is true and useless. The systematic version is a closed-form Monte Carlo of every primitive's weight over the crossings a camera actually sees — 22 estimators, four parameter families, every number cited to a run.</p>
      <p>Each analytic primitive samples some photon dimensions with a density <code>p</code>, sweeps two more into a sheet, and meets the camera ray at a crossing with weight</p>
    </div>
    <div class="formula">
      <div class="f">W = f / ( p · J ),   J = |(∂x/∂α × ∂x/∂β) · d|</div>
      <div class="n">and W = 0 when the sheet misses the ray. The per-pixel relative variance then comes from three places, and every finding in the study is one of them.</div>
    </div>
    <div class="narrow">
      <ul class="clean">
        <li><b>Miss mass.</b> With crossing probability <code>P</code>, the zero point-mass alone contributes <code>(1 − P)/P</code>. Measured as the <em>whole</em> story for the UV quad (rel std = 1.05–1.16 × √(1/P − 1) on 90% of pixels) and as the exponential wall of the photon sphere in dense fog.</li>
        <li><b>How J vanishes.</b> Constant across a pixel: a grazing band <em>between</em> pixels, no in-pixel tail. Linearly with the sampled coordinate (the planes): an integrable tail, mean converges everywhere. As the square root — a <strong>fold</strong>, two quadric roots merging (sphere, cone, and every hourglass): <code>W ~ ε^{−1/2}</code>, tail index 2, and <code>E[W²]</code> is <em>log-divergent</em>. The sample variance of a fold member never converges (the sphere's grows 5.2 → 20.1 from 10³ to 1.6·10⁷ samples) and must never be read as a convergence gauge. A Cauchy fan (the disk): bounded, but silent on two exact rays.</li>
        <li><b>Whether p tracks f.</b> Phase function, transmittance and emitter cosine are common multipliers — <em>unless</em> the phase peak sits on a member's singular locus. The same <code>g = 0.8</code> divides the sphere's variance by 23 and multiplies the disk's by 11 on identical Jacobian histograms.</li>
      </ul>
    </div>
    <div class="pair">
      <div class="pane"><img src="data:image/png;base64," width="1100" height="420" loading="lazy" decoding="async" alt="dirsweep_fig_var_vs_N.png" style="border-radius:10px;border:1px solid var(--line)"></div>
      <div class="pane"><img src="data:image/png;base64," width="1100" height="245" loading="lazy" decoding="async" alt="dirsweep_fig_phase_point.png" style="border-radius:10px;border:1px solid var(--line)"></div>
    </div>
    <div class="paircap"><b>Study figures</b><span>Left: the sample variance of the sphere and cone estimators keeps growing with N — the fold's log-divergent second moment, measured. Right: the same crossings under three phase functions; the sphere's fold sits at the phase minimum and the disk's fan at its maximum, so one <code>g</code> helps one member and hurts the other.</span></div>

    <div class="narrow">
      <h3>The hourglass verdict, by light size</h3>
      <p>The efficiency question between the two seeds has an answer, and it is not the Jacobian. The vertex members are <strong>light-trace-limited</strong>: at the baseline waist their light half succeeds on 1–2% of roots, and that is the whole 30–90× gap in coverage below. Their Jacobian term is actually 2–3× <em>smaller</em> than 20's, with no axial pathology.</p>
      <div class="tw"><table>
        <thead><tr><th>member</th><th>coverage</th><th>cv²</th><th>relvar</th><th>wins when</th></tr></thead>
        <tbody>
          <tr class="key"><td>20 light-seeded</td><td>0.738</td><td>8.2</td><td>11</td><td><b>point lights and emitters under ~10°</b> — nothing else exists there; worst at the paraxial focus (331), best just under the ball (4.2)</td></tr>
          <tr><td>22a entry-seeded</td><td>0.011</td><td>2.5</td><td>331</td><td>emitters over ~35°: overtakes 20 at edge 2.4 (27.6 vs 65); flat in ior</td></tr>
          <tr><td>23 exit cone</td><td>0.004</td><td>2.5</td><td>978</td><td>only low ior (≤ 1.2) with rays perpendicular to the axis; its back-trace through the ball loses coverage as ior rises</td></tr>
          <tr><td>24 reflection cone</td><td>0.003–0.006</td><td>1.7–10</td><td>450–2140</td><td><b>reflection caustics from emitters of edge ≥ ~1</b> — 1.3–50× the reflected beam; loses below edge 0.3</td></tr>
          <tr><td>18 beam, r = 0.01</td><td>0.110</td><td>0.14</td><td>9.3</td><td>as good as 20 at the waist; degrades linearly with the bundle radius; kernel-biased at the axial caustic</td></tr>
        </tbody>
      </table></div>
      <p class="note"><b>What the numbers say to do next.</b> Not MIS between the seeds — their densities live in different measures and the vertex members rarely have a root where 20 does. Importance-sample the light half instead: aim <code>θ</code> at the emitter and the 1–2% success rate is the entire gap. The medium, meanwhile, is irrelevant to the whole hourglass family (coverage 0.738 at every σ<sub>t</sub>).</p>
    </div>
    <div class="pair">
      <div class="pane"><img src="data:image/png;base64," width="1100" height="1047" loading="lazy" decoding="async" alt="fig_hg_lightsize.png" style="border-radius:10px;border:1px solid var(--line)"></div>
      <div class="pane"><img src="data:image/png;base64," width="1100" height="420" loading="lazy" decoding="async" alt="fig_hg_height.png" style="border-radius:10px;border:1px solid var(--line)"></div>
    </div>
    <div class="paircap"><b>Hourglass sweeps</b><span>Left: relative variance against emitter size for the four members — the crossover from 20 to 22a is where the emitter subtends ~35°. Right: camera height through the caustic; 20's spike at the paraxial focus is the axial line caustic sending every revolved sheet's <code>ρ → 0</code> at once.</span></div>
    <div class="narrow">
      <p>Six of the fifteen rules, each with its measurement in <code>docs/variance/README.md</code>: a single swept plane degrades like <code>sin(γ)^{−3}</code> in its angle to the camera; the three-plane mixture caps the worst pixel at 1.5 rel std in every viewing direction; never use the random-orientation plane when the continuous mixture exists (same samples, 1.6–2.2× better); the cone has an exact on/off criterion for bounded variance; the medium density matters only to members that sample a distance from it; and epsilon guards are irrelevant to variance — acceptance geometry and mixtures are what keep it finite.</p>
      <p>The study also records where its own Monte Carlo means did not match quadrature — a −0.7% cone clamp bias, the beam's kernel bias at the axial caustic, and a fold-tailed running mean sitting 31% high at 4·10⁵ samples before settling — so nobody has to rediscover them.</p>
    </div>
  </div>
</section>

<!-- ================= CORRELATED BATCH (slots after #variance, before #proof) ================= -->
<section id="batch" style="--secc:var(--l620)" data-nav="Seeing the estimator">
  <div class="wrap">
    <div class="narrow">
      <p class="sec-label">06 — What the estimator actually looks like</p>
      <h2>Freeze the batch and the maths becomes a photograph</h2>
      <p class="lead">Every estimator on this page samples a fresh primitive per camera sample, so the geometry averages away before you can see it. Reuse one batch across the whole frame instead and the individual swept sheets stay on screen — each weighted by its own co-area Jacobian, which is exactly the quantity the rest of this page is about.</p>
      <p>This is photon mapping's trick applied to analytic primitives, and it cost one line. The integrator already drew every photon-side random number <em>after</em> the camera ray was built, so correlating is a split of the random-number stream rather than a refactor: seed the photon side from the primitive index instead of the pixel, and every pixel that lands on index <code>k</code> rebuilds the same primitive bit for bit. Not one strategy block changed.</p>
    </div>

    <figure>
      <img src="data:image/png;base64," width="435" height="312" loading="lazy" decoding="async" alt="correlated/fig-cone-9.png" style="border-radius:10px;border:1px solid var(--line)">
      <figcaption><b>Sixteen photon cones, one apex</b><span>Each cone is one sample of the same estimator: a photon leaves the light at a fixed polar angle, and the azimuth and distance are swept into a surface. The camera ray meets that surface in closed form. Every cone shares the light as its apex, and the searing point where they all meet is not a bug in the render — it is the Jacobian going to zero at the tangency locus, which is the thing the mixture later has to fix.</span></figcaption>
    </figure>

    <div class="narrow">
      <h3>Each family fails in its own shape</h3>
      <p>The variance study classifies how each primitive's Jacobian vanishes — constant across a pixel, linearly, as a square-root fold, or as a bounded fan. That classification turns out to be literally a prediction about what the frozen batch looks like, because the Jacobian sits in the denominator.</p>
    </div>

    <div class="pair">
      <div class="pane"><img src="data:image/png;base64," width="435" height="312" loading="lazy" decoding="async" alt="correlated/fig-sphere-7.png" style="border-radius:10px;border:1px solid var(--line)"></div>
      <div class="pane"><img src="data:image/png;base64," width="435" height="312" loading="lazy" decoding="async" alt="correlated/fig-hourglass-20.png" style="border-radius:10px;border:1px solid var(--line)"></div>
    </div>
    <div class="paircap"><b>Fold members</b><span>Left, the photon sphere: a shell of constant flight distance about the light, and two quadric roots merge at its silhouette, so every bubble carries an incandescent rim. Right, the hourglass: sixteen caustic horns, and every one of them piles its brightest region onto the same axial line, because at the paraxial focus the revolution's Jacobian collapses for all of them at once.</span></div>

    <div class="narrow">
      <h3>The clearest argument for mixing anything</h3>
      <p>The balance heuristic changes a weight formula and draws no random numbers. So the two frames below are the <em>same frozen batch</em>, the same sixteen primitives in the same places, with only the edge weights different. Nothing about the geometry moved.</p>
    </div>

    <div class="pair">
      <div class="pane"><img src="data:image/png;base64," width="435" height="312" loading="lazy" decoding="async" alt="correlated/fig-mis-13-flat.png" style="border-radius:10px;border:1px solid var(--line)"></div>
      <div class="pane"><img src="data:image/png;base64," width="435" height="312" loading="lazy" decoding="async" alt="correlated/fig-mis-13-balance.png" style="border-radius:10px;border:1px solid var(--line)"></div>
    </div>
    <div class="paircap"><b>Flat weights, then balanced</b><span>Left: the three primitives averaged with equal weight — the rims are still there, because each member is still fully trusted on the locus where it is worst. Right: the balance heuristic, where a member's weight falls exactly where its own density spikes. The rims go out. This is the whole mixture argument in two frames that differ by one formula.</span></div>

    <div class="narrow">
      <div class="readout">
        <div class="row"><span class="lbl">Film maximum · cone alone</span><span class="val">49,000</span></div>
        <div class="row"><span class="lbl">Film maximum · three primitives, flat weights</span><span class="val">4,562</span></div>
        <div class="row hi"><span class="lbl">Film maximum · three primitives, balance heuristic</span><span class="val">368.7</span></div>
      </div>

      <h3>Two predictions that did not survive</h3>
      <p>The design document predicted a picture for each family before any of them was rendered. Most were right. Two were not, and they are worth more than the ones that were.</p>
      <ul class="clean">
        <li><b>The disk's pinwheel is unreachable.</b> Its blades are half-planes that <em>contain</em> the light's axis, so the pinwheel is what you would see looking straight down that axis — and every scene in this renderer has a level camera. From the side it is a fan of vertical blades, and level with the light it degenerates to two half-frames.</li>
        <li><b>The quad's tangency is one scanline, not scattered slivers.</b> The estimator translates the light quad without rotating it, so a ceiling quad stays horizontal at every distance and a level camera sees every member near edge-on at the same height. The whole estimator's variance lives on one row at the camera's eye level — which is also <em>why</em> its screen footprint is so small.</li>
      </ul>
      <p class="note"><b>The trap, fired deliberately.</b> The normalisation is one over the number of primitives <em>drawn</em>, never the number that crossed the ray. The wrong version was implemented behind a debug flag first, purely to watch it fail: it reads 2.1× to 6.8× too bright here, and it <em>converges</em> — 4.385, 4.447, 4.451 at rising pass counts on one preset. A quietly wrong image that looks more correct the longer you render it is the worst failure mode available, so it is now a thing this project has seen rather than a thing it was warned about.</p>
    </div>
  </div>
</section>


<!-- ================= SPEED ================= -->
<section id="speed" style="--secc:var(--l600)" data-nav="Speed">
  <div class="wrap">
    <div class="narrow">
      <p class="sec-label">06b — The speed</p>
      <h2>Blitzing fast, no neural network, no kernel on the sheet</h2>
      <p class="lead">Those three do not usually share a sentence about a volumetric caustic. Neural methods buy speed with a network; kernel methods buy it with blur; exact methods have been slow. The hourglass solves its sheet in closed form at the speed below. The word it does not get is <em>unbiased</em>: solo, its guard discards; paired, it carries the beam's kernel at weight O(r), and section 05's ladder says what that costs. The numbers below are what make the rest of the sentence true.</p>
      <div class="readout">
        <div class="row"><span class="lbl">Per pass — before</span><span class="val" style="color:var(--bad)">7.05 ms</span></div>
        <div class="row hi"><span class="lbl">Per pass — shipped</span><span class="val" style="color:var(--good)">1.17 ms</span></div>
        <div class="row"><span class="lbl">Film for these rows</span><span class="val">217×140 &middot; preset 48 &middot; strategy 20 &middot; CPU, i9-13980HX, 32 threads; the GPU only displays the film</span></div>
        <div class="row"><span class="lbl">Of which estimation</span><span class="val">0.76 ms</span></div>
        <div class="row"><span class="lbl">Rasterized gather, bit-identical to tracing</span><span class="val">quad 16.7× · beam 5.8× · hourglass 1.1× &mdash; it crosses half the frame, so there is nothing to skip</span></div>
      </div>
      <p style="margin-top:20px">The first row is worth a sentence, because it is the kind of number this project publishes rather than hides. Eighty-eight percent of a photon-primitive pass was the renderer waiting for a vertical blank: the window hardcoded a swap interval of one and drew one accumulation pass per frame, so every pass paid a display refresh against 0.76 ms of actual work. It was found by one measurement — a twenty-fold change in film size moved the per-pass cost by seven percent, so nothing inside the pass could own it — and fixed with a passes-per-frame budget. Thirty-three films, byte-identical before and after. The estimator had been fast all along; the display was hiding it. <b>How reproducible is a millisecond on this site?</b> Measured, and only once: the one cost column that has been run three times, interleaved, on a single binary holds to <b>4.4&ndash;9.1&nbsp;%</b> within a session, and moved by about <b>1.6&times;</b> between two sessions a day apart on this laptop (<span class="mono">docs/ring-arc/harness/ra_gate/cost.json</span>). Every wall-clock number on this site carries that precision, this one included. The ratios it is spent on &mdash; 7.05 against 1.17, 16.7&times; on the rasterised gather &mdash; are taken inside one session, which is the half of it that reproduces.</p>
      <p>The frame at the top of this page is the measurement. The Gate, preset 54, 363&times;505, strategy 21, 16,000 passes. Shot as a pixel-registered A/B at 6,000 passes against the stochastic beam at <code>r = 0.70</code>: the analytic side's waist peaks <b>5.3&times;</b> higher and its full width at half maximum is <b>7.7 px against 70</b>, while the two frames agree on total energy to 4&nbsp;%. Same transport, nine times sharper, at the same pass count &mdash; <b>against a beam given nearly five times the pair's radius.</b> A 1D kernel's width scales with its radius, so on 2026-09-08 the same frame was rendered with the beam at the pair's own radius, 16.1 px across the waist (14.1&ndash;18.2 over the band): at matched radius the pair's waist is the tighter by a factor of <b>2.0</b>, and the remaining 4.5 was the competitor's knob. The pair at a third of its radius, <code>r = 0.05</code>, stays at 7.5 px, so the waist is the sheet's and not the kernel's; its energy is where the kernel shows, and section 05 has that ladder. Both extra films are measured by the same producer over the same band and stored beside the four numbers below. <b>Two of those four numbers are a correction.</b> The readout published 4.4&times; and 57 px until 2026-09-08; those came from a hand reading whose row was never recorded, and the films measure neither at any row. <span class="mono">docs/tools/waist.py</span> is now the producer: it takes the peak and the full width at half maximum of every row in the seventeen-row waist band of the same two films this page inlines, and reports the band median with its row-to-row spread &mdash; peak ratio 5.3&times; (4.7&ndash;6.2 across the band), width 70 px (68.5&ndash;73.1) against 7.7 px (6.1&ndash;10.4), energy ratio 0.96003. The wall-clock of that frame is the one number this section does not yet print: it is what the recording below is for, and it goes in the caption the day it is shot.</p>
    </div>
    <div class="pair">
      <div class="pane"><span class="tag a">A · stochastic beam, r = 0.70</span><img src="data:image/png;base64," width="363" height="505" loading="lazy" decoding="async" alt="The same caustic gathered with a wide kernel: a soft lozenge with no waist"></div>
      <div class="pane"><span class="tag b">B · analytic pair, r = 0.15</span><img src="data:image/png;base64," width="363" height="505" loading="lazy" decoding="async" alt="The same caustic computed analytically: a needle-thin waist"></div>
    </div>
    <div class="paircap"><b>Preset 54, equal passes</b><span>The beam's 70-px smear and the hourglass pair's 7.7-px pinch, same scene, same camera, same number of passes. Neither frame has a denoiser, a neural network or a clamp on it; B carries a kernel too, at r = 0.15, and with the beam at the pair's own radius A's waist is 16.1 px.</span></div>
    <div class="narrow">
      <h3>What the photon-surface line of work reported, and what this adds</h3>
      <p>The idea of sweeping a photon's unused dimensions into an analytic manifold is not mine, and it is earlier: Bitterli and Jarosz's photon planes (2017) and Deng et al.'s photon surfaces (2019) proved the variance argument. They proved it at offline cost. The planes paper ran on sixteen Xeon threads, compared estimators at ten minutes each, and reports absolute times of hundreds to thousands of seconds per image, for a 2.4&ndash;40&times; variance reduction over photon beams. The surfaces paper publishes no wall-clock and no hardware at all; its results are equal-time variance ratios, and it shows individual spinning estimators with variance up to 1.8 million times path tracing before MIS tames them. It also names, in its own limitations, the regime it lacks a robust solution for: a medium interaction immediately after a surface event.</p>
      <p>This project does not implement either paper's primitive. Its swept planes are a different split of the same dimension count, and the published multi-scatter construction is structurally inexpressible in the class table this family is built on — the transport page says exactly where. What it shares with that work is the idea. What it adds is an implementation fast enough to show what the idea is worth: 1.17 ms a pass on a laptop's CPU cores with no GPU compute in the loop, a rasterized gather that is byte-identical to tracing, a MIS network whose weights are closed-form with no root-find, and a dielectric member — the hourglass — that lands the specular case of the regime the surfaces paper left open, and, paired with the beam, converging to 1.0000 against the beam at the same radius &mdash; consistent, with its radius-dependence measured at +0.9 %. No speed ratio against the published work is printed here, because the scenes, resolutions and hardware differ; the comparison that is fair is the one above, against the kernel estimator in the same renderer, and it is 9&times; in width at equal passes against the beam at r = 0.70 and a factor of 2.0 at the pair's own radius.</p>
    </div>
    <div class="vslot"><div class="vslot-h">video &middot; The Gate, converging — the recording</div><div class="vslot-r">Preset 54 (The Gate), integrator mode 9 (key 0).   </div>
</section>

<!-- ================= PROOF ================= -->
<section id="proof" style="--secc:var(--l620)" data-nav="Proof">
  <div class="wrap">
    <div class="narrow">
      <p class="sec-label">06 — How it was proven</p>
      <h2>Two independent estimators, or it didn't happen</h2>
      <p class="lead">Every primitive in the family had to divide against something it shares no code with, and land on 1.000. Every row that claims it has the run behind it; the ones that land elsewhere — the solo hourglass at 0.976, the beam at 1.048, the reflection cone at 0.998 — say so in the ledger, and the pair closes the first to 1.0000.</p>
      <ul class="clean">
        <li><b>Ratio against the oracle.</b> Each estimator renders the same configuration as the NEE reference until the per-pixel median ratio converges to 1.000. Median, not mean — a single firefly cannot hide a systematic error.</li>
        <li><b>Byte-identical regression.</b> The strongest test available, and the one that caught the most. A refactor that should not change the image must produce a bit-identical file; an extra random draw shifting the stream, or a gate that quietly became more permissive, shows up nowhere else.</li>
        <li><b>Degenerate limits as measure pins.</b> ior→1 collapses the hourglass onto the cone; σ→0 collapses a stochastic surface onto its mean. Limits where a new estimator becomes an old one are free, exact tests.</li>
        <li><b>Four-way derivation, then measurement.</b> The MIS density was derived independently four times before being compared against the sampler's empirical histogram. Agreement to 1.0007 — the derivation and the code were checked against each other, not against expectation.</li>
      </ul>
      <p class="note"><b>The habit that mattered most was negative.</b> Reasoning about why an image is dark does not work. One investigation ran for several rounds on careful inference, reached a confident wrong conclusion, and recorded it in a commit message as settled. A single counter in the actual code overturned it in one run: 27657 rays, 15131 hits, 63% correctly blocked. The bug was elsewhere. Instrument first.</p>
    </div>
  </div>
</section>

<!-- ================= LIMITS ================= -->
<section id="limits" style="--secc:var(--l680)" data-nav="Limits">
  <div class="wrap">
    <div class="narrow">
      <p class="sec-label">07 — What it does not do</p>
      <h2>The honest boundary</h2>
      <p class="lead">The scope is stated as precisely as the results, because a boundary you can name is what makes a result usable. These six are the boundary, and the first one is the thesis of the whole family.</p>
      <ul class="clean">
        <li><b>Not a better sampler for easy paths.</b> A swept primitive is more machinery than a light sample and a shadow ray, and on transport that was easy to sample to begin with, the machinery does not pay. Single scatter from an area light is the measured case: the camera walk's next-event estimate beats every swept member at every emitter size, 2.2 to 3.1× per pass. The family earns its cost on the paths that have no connection to make: the caustic through glass, where a connection would have to bend; the emitter too sharp to hit by sampling; the light source with more dimensions than a point sample can cover. There it lands what path sampling finds only by chance and what kernels can only blur. The hourglass is the proof; the sharp emitter and the volumetric light are the next two cases to measure.</li>
        <li><b>Medium-only.</b> Surfaces occlude and emit, but do not bounce. Walls look dark next to a full path tracer — that is the declared scope, and it is why every comparison here is against a medium-only reference that describes exactly the same transport.</li>
        <li><b>Straight-line primitives cannot refract.</b> Strategies 0–17 and the cross-family mixture at 26 are exact connections; none of them can bend at a dielectric interface. A glass ball under those estimators casts a correct shadow and no caustic. Neither can the one-dimensional group at 28&ndash;30, and there the failure is sharper than dimness: a smooth dielectric's emission profile is a two-dimensional delta, integrating a delta over one swept coordinate leaves a delta, and those three read <em>identically zero</em>. Structural, and the reason the hourglass exists. Strategy 27 is the one member that turns at a surface without being a dielectric &mdash; it reflects at a rough one, and still does not refract.</li>
        <li><b>The hourglass needs rotational symmetry, and now it is tested.</b> It is derived for spherical dielectrics: a glass box or a lens has no axis about which the refraction chain is invariant, and the derivation does not survive. The chain extension is the sharpest statement of that boundary, because it makes the condition <em>checkable at run time</em> — several balls are still one rigid motion if and only if every centre lies on the light-to-first-centre line, and the estimator tests that and refuses when it fails. It is also why the chain is a point-source result: a finite emitter moves the axis every sample. A fixed-apex form for the general case is derived and numerically validated; its light-side closure is measure-zero, and a standalone harness has since costed the general chain at fourteen to forty-two times one-ball strategy 20, which settles it as a no-go rather than an open problem.</li>
        <li><b>Solo, it is 2.4% low; paired, it is 1.0000.</b> The pairing with the stochastic beam, which carries internal-reflection chains at weight one, closes the gap: 0.976 → 1.0000. The attribution of the solo shortfall is not settled. The hourglass cannot express internal-reflection chains, which is the obvious explanation — but the grazing guard discards samples rather than clamping them, and the variance study measures it rejecting <em>2.4% of this strategy's energy at the waist</em> in the same configuration. The two candidate explanations are numerically the same size and have not been separated.</li>
        <li><b>Paired, it is consistent, not unbiased.</b> The pair's energy on the isolated caustic moves with the beam radius it carries — +0.9 % at r = 0.15, +1.9 % at r = 0.30, first order in r and resolved at 20 and 44 sigma on the paired bar — while the beam alone is flat in r to 0.2 %. Its waist does not move: 7.7 px at r = 0.15, 7.5 at r = 0.05 on the Gate. That is the same structure complement mode refuses strategy 30 for; the difference is that the pair's box is the one no other estimator can own, so it ships as the production primary with the number beside it rather than without it.</li>
      </ul>
    </div>
  </div>
</section>

<script>
(function(){
  var links = Array.prototype.slice.call(document.querySelectorAll('#rail a'));
  var secs  = links.map(function(a){ return document.getElementById(a.dataset.s); });
  var fill  = document.getElementById('railfill');
  var track = document.getElementById('railtrack');

  links.forEach(function(a){
    a.addEventListener('click', function(e){
      var t = document.getElementById(a.dataset.s);
      if (!t) return;
      e.preventDefault();
      t.scrollIntoView({ behavior:'smooth', block:'start' });
      if (history.replaceState) history.replaceState(null, '', '#' + a.dataset.s);
    });
  });

  function progress(){
    if (!fill || !track) return;
    var h = document.documentElement.scrollHeight - window.innerHeight;
    var p = h > 0 ? Math.min(1, Math.max(0, window.scrollY / h)) : 0;
    fill.style.height = (p * track.offsetHeight) + 'px';
  }
  var queued = false;
  window.addEventListener('scroll', function(){
    if (queued) return;
    queued = true;
    requestAnimationFrame(function(){ progress(); queued = false; });
  }, { passive:true });
  window.addEventListener('resize', progress, { passive:true });
  progress();

  if (!('IntersectionObserver' in window)) return;
  var io = new IntersectionObserver(function(entries){
    entries.forEach(function(e){
      var i = secs.indexOf(e.target);
      if (i < 0) return;
      links[i].classList.toggle('on', e.isIntersecting && e.intersectionRatio > 0.12);
    });
  }, { threshold:[0, .12, .5] });
  secs.forEach(function(s){ if (s) io.observe(s); });
})();
</script>
